title: Apply food safety practices in the perishable produce industry

lessons.title: Where contamination comes from and why it matters
lessons.html:
Sources of contamination in perishable produce

Fresh fruit and vegetables are usually eaten raw. There is no cooking step to kill germs or break down chemicals, so whatever gets onto the produce on the farm or in the packhouse can reach the consumer in Rotterdam, Dubai or Johannesburg. As a supervisor you must know the three groups of hazards and where each one comes from.

1. Biological hazards

  • Bacteria such as E. coli, Salmonella and Listeria, carried by dirty irrigation water, manure, animals and unwashed hands.
  • Viruses such as hepatitis A and norovirus, spread mainly by sick workers and poor toilet hygiene.
  • Moulds that rot fruit and, in some products, can produce toxins.

2. Chemical hazards

  • Pesticide residues above the maximum residue limit (MRL) of the importing country, usually because the pre-harvest interval on the label was not respected.
  • Post-harvest fungicides and waxes used at the wrong concentration.
  • Lubricants, fuel, cleaning chemicals and sanitisers that drip or splash onto fruit.

3. Physical hazards

  • Glass from broken light bulbs, hard plastic from crates, metal pieces from machinery, staples, jewellery, stones and wood splinters from pallets.

The effects of contamination

Contamination has effects at every level of the chain:

  • Consumers can get ill. Some foodborne bacteria cause serious illness, especially in young children, pregnant women and the elderly.
  • The business faces rejected consignments, product recalls, lost market access and damaged reputation. One residue failure can lead to every container from that exporter being tested at the port of entry.
  • The industry suffers when a market tightens rules for all South African fruit after repeated problems.

A residue problem found in Europe can often be traced back to one block, one spray and one person who did not check the label. That is why food safety is everybody's job, from the tractor driver to the packhouse manager.

lessons.title: Good agricultural practices on the farm
lessons.html:
Using GAP to prevent contamination in the orchard and field

Good agricultural practices (GAP) are the on-farm controls that stop hazards reaching the produce before it is even harvested. Export markets and retailers usually require a GAP certification such as GLOBALG.A.P., and the auditor will check both your practices and your records.

Water

  • Know the source of irrigation and spray water: borehole, river, dam or canal.
  • Have water tested for microbes at the intervals your certification scheme requires, especially where water touches the edible part.
  • Keep livestock and kraals away from water sources and irrigation dams.

Soil, manure and animals

  • Use only properly composted manure, applied well before harvest and never onto the fruit.
  • Keep cattle, goats and dogs out of the orchard during the harvest period. Fence where needed.

Agricultural remedies

  • Use only products registered under Act 36 of 1947 for that crop and that pest.
  • Follow the label for dose, number of applications and the pre-harvest interval.
  • Check that the product is accepted in the target market. Some actives allowed in South Africa have lower or zero MRLs overseas.
  • Record every spray: date, block, product, dose, operator and equipment.

Worker hygiene in the field

  • Provide clean toilets and hand-washing stations within reasonable walking distance of the pickers.
  • Train pickers to wash hands after the toilet and before handling fruit.
  • Sick workers with diarrhoea, vomiting or open wounds must report to the supervisor and be moved away from fruit.

Harvest equipment

  • Clean picking bags, ladders, crates and bins before the season and regularly during it.
  • Never place filled crates directly on soil or under trees with bird droppings.
  • Do not use harvest crates to carry fertiliser, chemicals or fuel.

GAP only works if it is written down, trained and checked. A supervisor who walks the rows each morning and looks at toilets, crates and spray records will prevent most problems.

lessons.title: GMP and hygiene management in the packhouse
lessons.html:
Good manufacturing practices in handling and storage

Once fruit arrives at the packhouse, good manufacturing practices (GMP) take over. GMP covers the building, the equipment, the people and the way product moves.

  • Building: intact roof and walls, no gaps where birds and rodents enter, covered or shatter-proof lights over the line.
  • Flow: raw fruit moves in one direction towards packed product, so that dirty bins do not cross paths with packed cartons.
  • Storage: packed product stored off the floor, away from chemicals, at the correct temperature.
  • Chemicals: cleaning agents and post-harvest products kept in a locked, labelled store and never above product.

Personal hygiene rules for packhouse staff

  • Wash and sanitise hands on entering the packing area and after breaks.
  • Wear clean overalls or aprons and hairnets. No jewellery except a plain wedding band if your policy allows it.
  • No eating, drinking, smoking or chewing gum on the line.
  • Cover cuts with a coloured, detectable plaster.

A hygiene management system

A hygiene management system turns these rules into a controlled process. Its main parts are:

  1. Written procedures for cleaning each area and machine: what chemical, what concentration, how often and who does it.
  2. Cleaning schedules and records signed by the cleaner and checked by the supervisor.
  3. Pest control with a site map of bait stations and insect traps, inspected and recorded by the pest control service.
  4. Glass and hard plastic register listing every item and its condition, checked regularly.
  5. Verification such as visual inspections, swab tests of food contact surfaces and internal audits.
  6. Corrective action when something fails: fix it, find the cause and record what was done.

If a glass bulb breaks over the line, stop the line, isolate the product in the area, clean up according to the procedure and record the incident before packing restarts. Never just sweep it away and carry on.

Key points

  • Hazards are biological, chemical or physical.
  • Contamination harms consumers and can close markets.
  • GAP controls water, manure, animals, sprays and field hygiene.
  • GMP controls the building, flow, storage and people in the packhouse.
  • A hygiene system needs procedures, records, verification and corrective action.

quiz.question: A piece of glass from a broken light found in a carton is an example of which kind of hazard?
What is the most common on-farm cause of pesticide residues above the importing country's MRL?

options.text: Not respecting the pre-harvest interval on the label

quiz.question: A picker reports that he has had diarrhoea since last night. What should the supervisor do?

options.text: Let him pick but tell him to wash his hands more
Ignore it unless he has a fever
Ask him to work in the packhouse instead
Move him away from handling fruit

quiz.question: Why is manure on fresh produce a particular concern?

options.text: It can carry harmful bacteria and fresh produce is often eaten raw

quiz.question: A light bulb breaks above the packing line. What is the correct first action?

options.text: Sweep up the glass and keep packing
Finish the shift and report it the next day
Stop the line and isolate product in the area
Replace the bulb and say nothing

quiz.question: Harvest crates may be used to carry fertiliser as long as they are rinsed afterwards.
Cleaning schedules should be signed by the cleaner and checked by the supervisor.
Which of these are parts of a packhouse hygiene management system? (select all that apply)

options.text: Pest control with a map of bait stations
A glass and hard plastic register
Allowing staff to eat at the packing line
